A few things help: put the crate beside your bed at first so he can see and smell you, give him a safe chew, tire him out before bed, and take him out quickly and calmly when he needs it, without playing.

A balanced approach: check for needs (pee, hunger, temperature) and respond to those, but don't let him out just because he's loud. Wait for a short pause in the crying before opening the door, so he's not rewarded for the noise. Cold-turkey 'cry it out' at 10 weeks is usually too much.

turns.user: how come treats work better than just telling him no when he does something wrong
turns.assistant:
Dogs learn by association and consequences. When a behavior is followed by something good, it becomes more likely. When it's followed by something unpleasant, they may stop it, but they don't understand what you want instead. 'No' only tells him what to stop, not what to do. A puppy who chews your shoe gets no information about the right thing to chew.

Rewarding the behaviors you want, such as chewing his toy, sitting calmly, or going to his crate, teaches what to do. Mistimed punishment can also create fear or confusion. A reward must come within a second or two of the behavior to link them.

turns.user: why does aquafaba whip up like egg whites? tried it last week with chickpea water and it actually worked but i dont get why
turns.assistant:
The liquid from cooked chickpeas contains proteins and starches, along with saponins and other compounds, that leach out during cooking. Like egg white proteins, these proteins unfold at the air-water interface and form a film around bubbles. The starches and sugars thicken the liquid so the bubbles are held in place.

That's why it makes a foam. Egg whites work with more protein, which sets when heated, while aquafaba is weaker but similar enough for meringues, mousse and macarons.

turns.user: and why did mine collapse when i added the sugar early
turns.assistant:
Sugar dissolves into the water phase and in the early stages interferes with the proteins forming a network around the bubbles. It also makes the liquid heavier, slowing the foam as it builds. If you add it all at the start, the foam struggles to form stiff peaks.

The usual approach is to whip the aquafaba to soft peaks first (it takes 8 to 10 minutes with a mixer), then add sugar gradually, a spoonful at a time. At that point the sugar helps stabilize the foam by making it glossy and firm. Add a little cream of tartar or lemon juice at the start for extra stability.

turns.user: is there a reason canned vs home cooked chickpeas matter
turns.assistant:
Yes. The concentration of the dissolved solids is the key factor. Canned chickpeas are cooked in a small amount of liquid under pressure, so the liquid is fairly thick and consistent. Home-cooked chickpeas are usually cooked in a lot of water, so the liquid is thinner and has fewer proteins per spoonful.

If you use homemade, simmer the liquid down until it's about the consistency of raw egg white, roughly a third to half of its volume. Salt in canned liquid is also a small factor, since too much slows foaming, so drain low-sodium cans if you can.

turns.user: and does the foam keep, like can i make it ahead
turns.assistant:
Not for long. Aquafaba foam deflates more quickly than egg white foam, especially when it's runny or sits in a warm kitchen. You can leave it a short time (maybe 15 to 20 minutes) before you use it, and rewhipping briefly can bring it back.

If you need to make ahead, bake the meringues or cookies and then store them airtight, since baked meringue is shelf-stable for days. Raw aquafaba liquid itself keeps in the fridge for about 5 days, or you can freeze it in ice cube trays.
